item.title: Cervical Central / Unilateral PA Mobilization
clinicalUse: Mechanical neck pain with segmental stiffness.
Painful or restricted cervical extension/rotation when neurological and vascular screening is clear.
Use as an adjunct when a comparable sign improves after a low-force trial.
patientPosition: Prone with forehead supported and cervical spine close to neutral.
Shoulders relaxed and arms comfortable beside the body.
If prone is poorly tolerated, use an alternative supported position rather than forcing the posture.
therapistPosition: Stand at the head or side of the table, close to the target segment.
Keep elbows soft and use body weight through relaxed shoulders.
stabilization: The table and patient position provide most of the stabilization.
Avoid excessive global neck movement; the contact should create a local accessory motion.
contact: Central PA: hypothenar/thumb contact over the spinous process of the selected vertebra.
Unilateral PA: contact over the articular pillar on the side being assessed/treated.
Use a broad comfortable contact and avoid painful fingertip pressure.
forceDirection: Force travels anteriorly through the selected segment for a PA mobilization.
Grade I–II for pain-dominant presentations; Grade III–IV when stiffness dominates and irritability is lower.
Oscillation should be smooth, rhythmic and in the same line throughout the set.
dosage: Common starting dose: 30–60 seconds of oscillation × 2–4 bouts.
Reassess after each bout rather than completing a fixed number regardless of response.
steps: 1. Record the comparable sign such as painful rotation or extension.
2. Screen for neurological deficit, instability, fracture risk and cervical vascular concerns.
3. Identify the segment that appears relevant to the comparable sign.
4. Apply a low-grade PA first and ask the patient to report pain quality and location.
5. Continue only if symptoms remain local and acceptable.
7. If movement improves, repeat or progress carefully and then add active cervical control/strength.
reassess: Functional task such as looking over shoulder
mistakes: Pushing the whole neck instead of the selected segment.
Using high grades before judging irritability.
Continuing despite dizziness, unusual headache or distal neurological symptoms.
safety: Do not perform when instability, fracture, acute inflammatory instability, severe neurological compromise or vascular pathology is suspected.
Cervical manual therapy requires appropriate contemporary vascular/neurological screening.
item.visualCue: Contact: spinous process/articular pillar → Force: PA (posterior-to-anterior) → Re-test cervical movement.

subTechniques.name: Cervical Central PA Mobilization
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Pain modulation or segmental extension tolerance when a central PA changes the patient's comparable sign.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Prone with the forehead supported and cervical spine close to neutral. Keep shoulders relaxed.
subTechniques.contact: Use a broad supported-thumb or hypothenar contact over the selected spinous process; avoid sharp fingertip pressure.
subTechniques.direction: Apply a smooth posterior-to-anterior oscillation through the selected segment. Grade I–II for pain-dominant presentations; Grade III–IV only when stiffness dominates and irritability is low.
subTechniques.dosage: 30–60 seconds × 2–4 bouts with immediate re-test after each bout.
subTechniques.reassess: Cervical extension/rotation, local pain and the patient's look-up/look-over-shoulder task.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: A central PA should create a local accessory movement—not rock the whole neck.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Stop with dizziness, unusual headache, neurological change or disproportionate symptom increase.

subTechniques.name: Cervical Unilateral PA Mobilization
subTechniques.target: Cervical articular pillar on the selected side
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve a painful/restricted rotation or extension comparable sign when unilateral segmental loading is helpful.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Prone with head supported and neck relaxed near neutral.
subTechniques.contact: Broad thumb/hypothenar contact over the articular pillar while the opposite hand supports the contact and head position.
subTechniques.direction: Apply a controlled posterior-to-anterior oscillation on the selected articular pillar.
subTechniques.reassess: Cervical rotation to the symptomatic side, extension and referred symptom behavior.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Re-test after the first short bout. If the comparable sign does not change, do not simply increase force.

subTechniques.name: Lower-Cervical Side Glide
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve selected lateral translation restriction or modify a radicular/mechanical comparable sign.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the head fully supported in neutral or slight flexion.
subTechniques.contact: Cradle the neck and contact the lateral articular pillar/segment with a broad hand surface.
subTechniques.direction: Translate the selected cervical segment gently sideways while minimizing rotation and flexion/extension.
subTechniques.dosage: 20–40 seconds × 2–4 bouts or small oscillations, staying below symptom aggravation.
subTechniques.reassess: Cervical side-bending/rotation and upper-limb symptom distribution.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: A useful side glide often changes the arm symptom or neck movement immediately; if not, reconsider the hypothesis.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Do not continue if arm symptoms peripheralize or neurological findings worsen.
